Mahima had been in Bengaluru three months when she opened her tiffin of theplas and methi pickle at the office lunch table. A man from the sales team wrinkled his nose. "Wow. Gujju smell. Do you people eat anything without sugar?"

A few people laughed. Mahima's cheeks went hot, and under the heat came anger. For a moment she wanted to shut the tiffin and never bring it again.

Instead she looked up and said evenly, "It's my mother's recipe. You're welcome to try one, or not." Then she went on eating.

Nikita, from her own team, pulled a chair closer. "Can I try? My flatmate's from Surat, she makes these." She took one and said, loudly, "These are brilliant."

That week Mahima brought extra theplas. She kept eating at the same table. And when the man walked past, she didn't lower her eyes.

qa.a: Mahima's tiffin had theplas and methi pickle.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when the man mocked her food?
qa.a: Mahima felt small and angry, her cheeks going hot, and was tempted to hide her tiffin.

qa.q: How did Mahima respond, and why did it work?
qa.a: She answered calmly, kept eating, found an ally in Nikita and kept bringing her food, staying proud instead of withdrawing.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt watching the man mock Mahima's food?
qa.a: Nikita likely felt uncomfortable and protective, which is why she moved closer and praised the theplas loudly.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose food draws a snide remark in a new city, answering calmly, finding an ally and staying proud of her background.

"Abhinav, in this building we wear proper clothes on the stairs," said Irawati aunty, the landlady, eyeing his mundu. "This lungi business is fine for Kerala."

Abhinav felt the heat climb his neck. "Aunty, it's a mundu. It's what I wear at home."

"People will think you're a servant."

He took a breath. "People can think what they like. I'm going to buy milk. Good evening."

On the stairs he met Farhan, the neighbour from Lucknow. "She said something about your mundu, na? She told me my kurta was 'village style' last month."

"I wanted to say something rude."

"Don't. Come to the Onam lunch at the Malayali Samajam on Sunday. You can wear it there and everyone will be jealous."

Abhinav laughed, and the anger loosened. He wore the mundu to the shop and back, head up.

Vaibhav, you asked me on the show what nobody tells you after the big goal. It's Chandrika here, twenty-two, and last year I did everything right. Engineering degree, campus placement, the job in the glass building. My parents distributed sweets. And by March I was lying on my bed every evening scrolling until two, wondering: is this it? What is any of this for?

I kept waiting to find my purpose, like it was a lost wallet.

What changed was small. A colleague asked me to cover her Saturday slot at a children's reading hour in the public library. I went, grumbling. A boy of eight read a whole page aloud for the first time and looked at me like I'd given him a medal.

I went back the next Saturday. Then I tried a pottery class, which I was terrible at. I'm still trying things. Purpose didn't arrive. It's growing, one Saturday at a time.

qa.a: Chandrika felt empty and lost, scrolling until two and wondering what everything was for.

July. Darshan had his degree, a certificate in a plastic sleeve, and no idea what came next. He woke at noon in his parents' flat in Vadodara, scrolled short videos until evening, and felt nothing much at all.

August, a Wednesday. Hansa ben, who ran the community kitchen in the temple compound, caught him on the stairs. "You have free hands. We are short of people to chop vegetables on Wednesdays." He said yes mostly to escape.

October. He had not missed a Wednesday. He'd learned to cut onions without crying, and an old man named Mohanbhai told him stories about the textile mills while they worked. Last week, Hansa ben asked him to help set up a spreadsheet for donations. He stayed three hours. On the bus home he realised he hadn't opened the video app all day.

He still didn't know what his life was for. But Wednesdays had a point.

I'm Ankita, and for two years I pretended to want to be a chartered accountant. Papa is one, and Dadaji was one, and our family's office sign in Indore has space for my name. I went to the coaching classes. I failed the intermediate once and felt relief, which scared me.

What I actually love is animation. I've been drawing short films on my old laptop at night since I was fourteen. Rashmi, my friend from school, saw them and said, "You can't keep living someone else's plan."

So in December I made a plan of my own. I showed Papa my films, a one-year animation diploma with fees I'd researched, and a fallback: I'd finish the CA foundation too, so a door stayed open.

Papa was quiet for a long time. Mummy cried. Papa said, "I'm worried." I said, "I know." It's not settled. But I'm not pretending anymore.

qa.a: Ankita draws short animated films on an old laptop at night.

qa.a: Ankita felt relief, which was scary because it showed how much the CA path felt like someone else's dream.

Mentor's note, second-year engineering, Pune.

Francis came to my office hour for the third time this month, again without questions about circuits. Today he admitted it: he has no interest in electronics. His parents chose the course. His father drives an auto and saved for years for the fees, and Francis feels "like a fraud every single day".

What Francis loves is carpentry. He showed me photos on his phone: a bookshelf with hidden joints, a cradle for his cousin's baby. His hands moved while he talked.

I didn't tell him what to do. We worked through options: finishing the degree while taking a furniture design certificate on weekends, or switching to a design course next year with a clear fallback. He decided to talk to his parents on Sunday, with the plan written down, and said he expected his mother to cry.

He'll come back next week to tell me how it went. - Gargi

qa.a: Francis made a cradle for his cousin's baby.

qa.q: How does Francis feel about studying electronics?

Monday night

Kavitha got into the design master's in Ahmedabad. Tiwari uncle's son got his bank job. Even Chotu from my building has a startup, apparently. I scrolled through everyone's announcements tonight and felt like I was standing still in a moving train. I'm Sachin, I'm twenty-one, and I have no idea what I want.

Then I called Kavitha to say congratulations, and she said something I didn't expect. "Honestly, I applied because I didn't know what else to do. I'm terrified." She said half our batch is guessing.

So those posts are the highlight reel. Not the whole film.

New rule for myself: no more comparing my messy middle to their best moments. Instead, try things. This Saturday, a free coding workshop at the library. Next month, maybe the photography walk. I'll follow whatever I keep thinking about afterwards.

I'm Mahima, and last month I did something that felt bold. I asked Pema-la, the senior architect at my internship, how she knew what she wanted to do. She's fifty-something, calm, respected. I expected a neat answer.

She laughed. "I didn't. I studied chemistry first. Then I taught school in Darjeeling for three years. Then I drew houses for fun and someone asked me to design theirs. I changed course three times, and the third one stuck."

I felt stunned. And something unclenched in my chest. I had been waiting to be sure before choosing anything, like certainty was a ticket I needed to board the train.

Now I'm collecting stories instead of formulas. I've asked four more people. None of them had a straight line. My plan now is to keep walking, and let the direction show itself along the way.

qa.a: Pema-la studied chemistry first.

Career centre counsellor's note, final-year students.

Damini has come to three talks this term and always sits in the front row with a notebook. Today's speaker was Dr Rao, a marine biologist who now runs a children's science theatre. After the talk, Damini waited in the queue for twenty minutes and asked her, "How did you know?"

Dr Rao said she didn't. She had trained as a dentist, left, worked in a bookshop, then studied biology at twenty-nine. Three changes of course in all.

I watched Damini's face. She looked surprised, then almost relieved. Later she told me, "I've been waiting to feel certain before I apply for anything."

We agreed she would stop waiting and apply for two different summer programmes, one in research and one in outreach, and see which one pulls her. She also plans to ask three more professionals about their paths.

- Sunaina

Sudha beti, you're reading that philosophy book every night now, yes? Good. Let your Irfan nana tell you about when I was twenty and lost. My father had died, I'd failed my exams, and nothing made sense. I started going to a Sufi poetry circle on Thursdays, in an old house near the dargah. We read Rumi and Bulleh Shah and argued about them over tea.

The poems comforted me. They also annoyed me, questioned me, kept me awake. The old teacher never gave answers. He only said, "What do you think it means?"

There was another group nearby with a man who had an answer for everything. My friend Salim went there. He became very sure, very fast, and stopped asking anything at all.

I stayed with the questions. I still have them. They've been better company than certainty.

Tushar, since your podcast is about being twenty-two and lost, here's mine. I'm Reena. For about a year I called myself lazy every morning. Lazy, useless, wasted my best years. I dropped out of my MBA prep, I slept till eleven, I watched my college friends post about jobs. I thought if I was harsh enough, I'd shock myself into working.

It did nothing. I just felt worse.

What shifted it was my cousin asking, "Are you lazy, or are you exhausted?" I cried, because I was so tired. Tired in a way sleep didn't fix. She took me to a counsellor. The counsellor said to stop labelling myself and take one tiny step a day.

My first step was making my bed. Pathetic, right? No. It was the first thing I'd finished in months. Now I'm doing an online course. Slowly. Kindly.

February. Sarika sat in her room in Lucknow, surrounded by unopened government-exam guides. Third attempt coming up, and she hadn't studied in weeks. In her notebook she wrote: You are lazy. You wasted your twenties. Everyone is ahead of you.

April, a Tuesday. Bhavna, her old hostel roommate, visited and found the notebook open. She read it and went quiet. "You wouldn't say this to me." Sarika shrugged. "You're not a failure." Bhavna put a hand on her arm. "You look exhausted, not lazy. You've looked like this for months. Will you see someone?"

May. Sarika had seen the college counsellor twice. They had agreed on one tiny step a day: fifteen minutes of reading, a walk to the corner shop, a call to Bhavna. Some days she only managed one. On the notebook's next page she wrote: Tired. Trying. That's enough for today.

Dear Deepika,

I've started this letter six times. Last Thursday I forwarded your private message about your family to the whole project group by mistake, and then, when you asked, I lied and said someone hacked my phone. That second part is what I can't forgive myself for.

Since then there's a voice in my head all day: you're worthless, you're a terrible person. I stopped eating properly. I almost stopped coming to class so I wouldn't have to see you.

But hiding isn't fair to you. So here is the truth. I forwarded it. I lied because I was ashamed. I'm sorry for both.

I've asked everyone in the group to delete it, and I've told our professor what happened, in case anyone misuses it. I did a bad thing. I'm trying to be someone who doesn't repeat it.

Siddharth

Jasleen, you asked about the worst week of my college life. It's Tushar speaking, so be kind. Second year, I was the mess secretary. I forgot to renew the gas cylinder order. On a Friday night two hundred students had no dinner. People were furious. Someone wrote my name on the notice board with a cross through it.

That night I lay awake and the voice was loud: you're useless, you're a waste of space, everyone hates you. I thought about quitting, not just the post, college.

My warden called me in the next morning. He said, "You made a serious mistake. You're not a serious mistake." Separating those two changed everything.

So I owned it. I apologised in the mess, in front of everyone. I set up a shared order calendar with two other students so it couldn't depend on one person. And I talked to myself like I'd talk to my younger brother. Firm, but kind.

Vinita's stomach dropped. The date had slipped past in exam week. "I did. I'm really sorry. There's no excuse."

Last month I snapped at Ishita, the new intern, in front of the whole design team. She'd sent the wrong file to a client. I said, "Did you even read the brief?" in a voice I didn't recognise. She went red and didn't speak for the rest of the day.

I'm Kalyani, and my old habit would have been to spiral. I'm a terrible manager, I'm a terrible person, I should quit. And then, out of shame, avoid her for a week.

This time I tried something my counsellor taught me. I said to myself: I made a mistake, and I'm still a person worth respect. That made it possible to walk to her desk the next morning.

"I was harsh yesterday. That wasn't okay. The file mistake was small and fixable; the way I spoke wasn't." She nodded, surprised.

Being kind to myself isn't a free pass. I've told my team lead about it, and I pause before giving feedback now.

In the courtyard of the university in Buenos Aires, Clara sat down next to Camila on the stone bench. Three weeks ago Camila had told their friends about Clara's parents' divorce, a secret Clara had trusted her with. Clara hadn't spoken to her since.

"I forgive you," Clara said. "I'm still hurt. But I forgive you."

Camila's eyes filled. Relief flooded her, and right behind it, a heavy feeling that she didn't deserve this. "Thank you. I don't think I've earned it."

"Maybe not yet," Clara said, almost smiling.

Camila wanted to hug her, to make everything normal right away. She didn't. She only said, "I won't ask you for anything more. I'll just show you."

Over the next weeks she kept every small promise. When friends gossiped about someone else's family, Camila changed the subject. Clara noticed.

The chemistry lab smelled of ethanol and burnt sugar. Jeevan waited by Salma's bench while she washed glassware. Last month he had presented her titration data as his own at the department seminar. When she found out, she went to their professor. Jeevan had apologised to both of them the same week.

Now Salma dried her hands. "I've been thinking. I forgive you, Jeevan."

He felt his knees go loose. Relief, and under it a hot shame. "I don't know if I deserve that."

"It's not a reward. I'm just tired of carrying it."

He nodded. He wanted to ask if they could be lab partners again, if she'd write with him on the paper. He stopped himself. That was hers to offer, not his to ask.

"Thank you," he said. "I'll make sure your name is first on anything we share." Then he went back to his own bench.

qa.q: What did Jeevan present as his own at the seminar?
qa.a: Jeevan presented Salma's titration data as his own.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when Salma said she forgave him?
qa.a: Jeevan felt relief, his knees going loose, and under it a hot shame that he didn't deserve it.

qa.q: What choice showed that Jeevan was not treating forgiveness as a reset?
qa.a: Jeevan stopped himself from asking to be partners again and instead promised to credit Salma first, leaving any further steps to her.

qa.q: How does Salma see her forgiveness?
qa.a: Salma sees it as a way to stop carrying the hurt, not as a reward for Jeevan or a return to how things were.

grounding: The lab scene shows a young man forgiven by the person he harmed, accepting humbly, not demanding more and changing his behaviour.
